A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Diffusion2 by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across substantial restructuring.

before.justification: v3 reports original generation experiments, a 50-participant user study, quantitative video-to-4D comparisons, schedule ablations and partial-reconstruction results in Appendix A.5.

after.justification: v4 reports original generation experiments, a 50-participant user study, quantitative video-to-4D results and component ablations, with additional visual results in Appendix A.6.

M1.justification: v4 introduces variance-reducing sampling with early denoising rollbacks and replaces the logistic score schedule with constant weighting of 0.5. Reconstruction changes from v3's 4D Gaussian Splatting formulation to canonical Gaussians with an MLP deformation field, a static warm-up and decoupled texture/dynamics optimization (Sections 3.3–3.4). These substantially revise both stages.

E1.justification: Image-to-4D and video-to-4D evaluation remain. However, v3's Objaverse static-3D animation experiments, explicit text-to-4D demonstrations and six-model partial-reconstruction benchmark using joint video/multi-view conditions disappear. v4 still mentions these input extensions conceptually, but its reported experiments concentrate on image/video conditions.

E2.justification: Table 1 replaces Animate124 with Consistent4D, STAG4D and Efficient4D while retaining DreamGaussian4D as DG4D. Table 2 removes 4DGen and adds STAG4D and DG4D alongside retained Consistent4D/Efficient4D; DG4D previously appeared only qualitatively in this task. v4 Figures 4 and 8 also introduce SV4D comparisons.

E3.justification: Video evaluation changes from averaging CLIP similarity over four rendered views to evaluating four novel views plus the input view, with LPIPS and FVD added. The user study changes from eight to eleven cases and three to five candidates, retaining 50 participants; reference consistency replaces the detail criterion. These materially change evaluation design and score comparability.

E4.justification: v3's logistic-parameter and schedule ablations are replaced by qualitative tests of VRS, score composition against independent SV3D generation and attention blending, and decoupled reconstruction. v4 also visualizes the models' differing predictions at the fourth denoising step (Figures 5–6), adding evidence about a proposed failure mechanism.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Both report point estimates and preference percentages from 50 participants. Changes to survey cases and candidates affect evaluation design, not uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces the reported results: Diffusion2 changes from CLIP 0.94 and 10 minutes to CLIP 0.922, LPIPS 12.35, FVD 1304.18 and 12 minutes under revised conditions. These are not matched-setting performance changes. User-study percentages and rankings also change, new qualitative results appear, and v3's partial-reconstruction PSNR/SSIM table is removed.

T1.justification: The score-composition theorem, conditional-independence assumption, noisy-data corollary and continuity-based weaker-assumption proof are retained. The main proof moves to v4 Appendix A.3, and the general-case argument moves to A.4. Explicitly restating existing factorizations and adding heuristic VRS motivation do not establish a new formal result.

C1.justification: The central claim of composing existing video and multi-view priors without 4D training data remains. However, v4's abstract and contribution list add VRS as a solution to conflicting scores and elevate decoupled reconstruction to a proposed contribution. The introduction also explicitly claims priority for practical training-free, single-pass multi-view video sampling.

C2.justification: v4 explains ghosting through disagreement between learned distributions and attributes texture loss partly to aggressive VRS, with decoupled reconstruction offered as a remedy. v3 primarily attributed such failures to foundation-model limitations. v4 also explicitly distinguishes parallelism's latency benefit from throughput and memory costs. The earlier discussion of inherited bias, copyright and employment impacts is removed.

D1.justification: v4 adds sampler pseudocode, the first-five-step rollback specification, a 3,000-iteration static warm-up, explicit evaluation azimuths and a survey template. Conversely, v3's FreeInit-inspired condition-generation recipe, view-dependent weighting formula and explicit confidence-weighted reconstruction objective are no longer documented. Their omission alone does not establish that every underlying operation was discontinued.

R1.justification: The 4D discussion adds works including SV4D, L4GM, Animate3D, Diffusion4D and SC4D, and more explicitly contrasts training-free composition with approaches requiring training. v3's stated inspiration from MultiDiffusion and SyncDiffusion, including those citations, disappears. These update positioning while retaining most of the broader 3D/video background.

P1.justification: Beyond the title change, v4 substantially rewrites the introduction and method narrative, separates the method into four subsections and moves the main proof into the appendix. Experiments are reorganized from task-based reporting into qualitative and quantitative comparisons, and the appendix structure is extensively revised.

P2.justification: v4 replaces the opening visualization, restructures Tables 1–2 with methods as columns, redesigns qualitative comparisons and replaces the schedule-ablation display. It adds a conditional-independence schematic, denoising-mode visualization, survey illustration and RGB/depth galleries, while removing the static-3D, text-to-4D and partial-reconstruction displays. Typography and page layout also change throughout.

improvement.justification: Compared with v3's schedule-focused ablations and CLIP-only video evaluation, v4 more directly tests score composition and reconstruction choices and adds perceptual and temporal metrics. Sampler pseudocode and explicit memory/throughput limitations also improve clarity. These benefits are partly offset by removing text/static-3D demonstrations, the partial-reconstruction benchmark and some implementation detail. The net quality improvement is limited; changed evaluation settings do not establish a direct performance gain.
